Deity - Wikipedia

Deity
A
deity
is a
supernatural
being considered to have authority over some aspect of the universe and/or life, with many also being considered as
sacred
and worthy of
worship
.
[
1
]
It is "a spirit or being believed to have created, or to control some part of the
universe
or life, for which such a deity is often worshipped".
[
2
]
The
Oxford Dictionary of English
explains
deity
as anything revered as
divine
.
[
3
]
While,
C. Scott Littleton
defines a deity as "a being with powers greater than those of ordinary humans, but who interacts with humans, positively or negatively, in ways that carry humans to new
levels of consciousness
, beyond the grounded preoccupations of ordinary life".
[
4
]
Various cultures have conceptualized their deities differently.
[
5
]
[
6
]
and may refer to their deities in a variety of ways—male, female,
androgynous
, or genderless.
[
7
]
[
8
]
[
9
]
A male deity is called a
god
, while a female deity is called a
goddess
.
Belief in the existence of at least one deity, who may interact with the world, is called
theism
.
[
10
]
Theistic beliefs can be categorized by how many deities they worship: whereas
polytheism
accept multiple deities,
[
11
]
monotheism
accept only one deity,
[
12
]
[
13
]
and
henotheism
accepts one supreme deity without denying other deities, considering them as aspects of the same divine principle.
[
14
]
[
15
]
Nontheistic religions
deny any supreme eternal
creator deity
, but may accept a
pantheon
of deities which live, die and may be reborn like any other being.

35–37

.
Many cultures—including the ancient
Mesopotamians
,
Egyptians
,
Greeks
,
Romans
, and
Germanic peoples
—have personified
natural phenomena
, variously as either deliberate causes or effects.
[

[

]
Some

and

deities were viewed as ethical concepts.
[

[

, deities have been envisioned as manifesting within the temple of every living being's body, as sensory organs and mind.

Etymology
The English language word
deity
derives from
Old French
deité
,
[
24
]
[
page
needed
]
the
Latin
deitatem
(nominative
deitas
) or "divine nature", coined by
Augustine of Hippo
from
deus
("god"). Deus is related through a common
Proto-Indo-European
(PIE) origin to
*deiwos
.
[
25
]
This root yields the ancient Indian word
Deva
meaning "to gleam, a shining one", from *div- "to shine", as well as
Greek
dios
"
divine
" and
Zeus
; and Latin
deus
"god" (
Old Latin
deivos
).
[

[

]
[

:

Deva is masculine, and the related feminine equivalent is
devi
.
[
29
]
:

Etymologically, the cognates of
Devi
are Latin
dea
and Greek
thea
.
[
30
]
In
Old Persian
,
daiva-
means "
demon
, evil god",
[
27
]
while in

[

:

The closely linked term "

Proto-Germanic
*
guthan

*
ghut-
, which means "that which is invoked".
[

:

Guth
in the

means "voice". The term
*
ghut-
is also the source of
Old Church Slavonic
zovo
("to call"), Sanskrit
huta-
("invoked", an epithet of
Indra
), from the root
*
gheu(e)-
("to call, invoke."),
[

]
An alternate etymology for the term "god" comes from the Proto-Germanic
Gaut
, which traces it to the PIE root
*
ghu-to-
("poured"), derived from the root
*
gheu-
("to pour, pour a
libation
"). The term
*
gheu-
is also the source of the Greek
khein
"to pour".
[

]
Originally the word "god" and its other Germanic cognates were
neuter
nouns but shifted to being generally masculine under the influence of Christianity in which the
god is typically seen as male
.
[

:

[

In contrast, all ancient
Indo-European cultures
and
mythologies
recognized both masculine and feminine deities.

Definitions
There is no universally accepted consensus on what a deity is, and concepts of deities vary considerably across cultures.
[
36
]
:
69–74
[
37
]
Huw Owen
states that the term "deity or god or its equivalent in other languages" has a bewildering range of meanings and significance.
[
38
]
:
vii–ix
It has ranged from "infinite transcendent being who created and lords over the universe" (God), to a "finite entity or experience, with special significance or which evokes a special feeling" (god), to "a concept in religious or philosophical context that relates to nature or magnified beings or a supra-mundane realm", to "numerous other usages".
[
38
]
:
vii–ix
A deity is typically conceptualized as a supernatural or divine concept, manifesting in ideas and knowledge, in a form that combines excellence in some or all aspects, wrestling with weakness and questions in other aspects,
heroic
in outlook and actions, yet tied up with emotions and desires.
[
39
]
[
40
]
In other cases, the deity is a principle or reality such as the idea of "soul". The
Upanishads
of Hinduism, for example, characterize
Atman
(soul, self) as
deva
(deity), thereby asserting that the
deva
and eternal supreme principle (
Brahman
) is part of every living creature, that this soul is spiritual and divine, and that to realize self-knowledge is to know the supreme.
[
41
]
[
42
]
[

]
Theism
is the belief in the existence of one or more deities.
[
44
]
[
45
]
Polytheism
is the belief in and worship of multiple deities,
[
46
]
which are usually assembled into a
pantheon
of gods and
goddesses
, with accompanying
rituals
.
[
46
]
In most polytheistic religions, the different gods and goddesses are representations of forces of nature or
ancestral principles
, and can be viewed either as autonomous or as aspects or
emanations
of a creator God or
transcendental
absolute principle
(
monistic
theologies), which manifests
immanently
in nature.
[
46
]
Monotheism
is the belief that only one deity exists.

A monotheistic deity is usually described as
omnipotent
,
omnipresent
,
omniscient
,
omnibenevolent
and
eternal
.
[

]
[
55
]
[

]
However, not all deities have been regarded this way
[

]
[

]
[

]
[

and an entity does not need to be almighty, omnipresent, omniscient, omnibenevolent or eternal to qualify as a deity.

[

Monotheistic religions typically refer to their god in masculine terms.

A similar concept,
monolatry
, while accepting that many deities exist, believes that only one of these deities may be validly worshipped.
[
61
]
[

]
Henotheism
, accepts the existence of more than one deity, but considers all deities as equivalent representations or aspects of the same divine principle, the highest.
[

]
[

[

]

Some philosophical forms of monotheism or henotheism, known as
classical theism
go a step further and precisely
identify the worshiped deity with Being itself
as a metaphysical grounds for the above attributes.
Deism
is the belief that only one deity exists, who created the universe, but does not usually intervene in the resulting world.
[
65
]
[
66
]
[
67
]
[
page

]
Deism was particularly popular among western intellectuals during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
[
68
]
[

]
Pantheism
is the belief that the universe itself is God
[
34
]
or that everything composes an all-encompassing,
immanent
deity.
[
35
]
Pandeism
is an intermediate position between these, proposing that the creator became a pantheistic universe.
[
70
]
Panentheism
is the belief that
divinity
pervades the universe, but that it also
transcends
the universe.
[
71
]
Agnosticism
is the position that it is impossible to know for certain whether a deity of any kind exists.
[
72
]
[
73
]
[

]
Atheism
is the non-belief in the existence of any deity.
[

Prehistoric
Scholars infer the probable existence of deities in the prehistoric period from inscriptions and prehistoric arts such as
cave drawings
, but it is unclear what these sketches and paintings are and why they were made.
[
78
]
Some engravings or sketches show animals, hunters or rituals.
[
79
]
It was once common for archaeologists to interpret virtually every prehistoric female figurine as a representation of a single, primordial goddess, the ancestor of historically attested goddesses such as
Inanna
,
Ishtar
,
Astarte
,
Cybele
, and
Aphrodite
;
[
80
]
this approach has now generally been discredited.
[
80
]
Modern archaeologists now generally recognize that it is impossible to conclusively identify any prehistoric figurines as representations of any kind of deities, let alone goddesses.
[
80
]
Nonetheless, it is possible to evaluate ancient representations on a case-by-case basis and rate them on how likely they are to represent deities.
[
80
]
The
Venus of Willendorf
, a female figurine found in Europe and dated to about 25,000
BCE has been interpreted by some as an exemplar of a prehistoric female deity.
[
79
]
A number of probable representations of deities have been discovered at
'Ain Ghazal
[
80
]
and the works of art uncovered at
Çatalhöyük
reveal references to what is probably a complex mythology.
[
80
]
Religions and cultures
Diverse African cultures developed theology and concepts of deities over their history. In
Nigeria
and neighboring
West African countries
, for example, two prominent deities (locally called
Òrìṣà
)
[
81
]
are found in the
Yoruba religion
, namely the god
Ogun
and the goddess
Osun
.
[
81
]
Ogun is the primordial masculine deity as well as the archdivinity and guardian of occupations such as tools making and use, metal working, hunting, war, protection and ascertaining equity and justice.
[
82
]
[
83
]
Osun is an equally powerful primordial feminine deity and a multidimensional guardian of fertility, water, maternal, health, social relations, love and peace.
[
81
]
Ogun and Osun traditions were brought into the Americas on
slave ships
. They were preserved by the Africans in their plantation communities, and their festivals continue to be observed.
[
81
]
[
82
]
In
Southern African cultures
, a similar masculine-feminine deity combination has appeared in other forms, particularly as the Moon and Sun deities.
[
84
]
One Southern African cosmology consists of
Hieseba
or
Xuba
(deity, god),
Gaune
(evil spirits) and
Khuene
(people). The
Hieseba
includes
Nladiba
(male, creator sky god) and
Nladisara
(females, Nladiba's two wives). The Sun (female) and the Moon (male) deities are viewed as offspring of
Nladiba
and two
Nladisara
. The Sun and Moon are viewed as manifestations of the supreme deity, and worship is timed and directed to them.
[
85
]
In other African cultures the Sun is seen as male, while the Moon is female, both symbols of the godhead.
[
86
]
:

In
Zimbabwe
, the supreme deity is
androgynous
with male-female aspects, envisioned as the giver of rain, treated simultaneously as the god of darkness and light and is called
Mwari Shona
.
[

]
:
89
In the
Lake Victoria
region, the term for a deity is
Lubaale
, or alternatively
Jok
.
[
87
]
Ancient Egyptian
culture revered numerous deities. Egyptian records and inscriptions list the names of many whose nature is unknown and make vague references to other unnamed deities.
[
89
]
:

James P. Allen
estimates that more than 1,400 deities are named in Egyptian texts,
[
90
]
whereas Christian Leitz offers an estimate of "thousands upon thousands" of Egyptian deities.
[
91
]
:
393–394
Their terms for deities were
nṯr
(god), and feminine
nṯrt
(goddess);
[
92
]
:
42
however, these terms may also have applied to any being – spirits and deceased human beings, but not demons – who in some way were outside the sphere of everyday life.
[

]
:
216
[
92
]
:

Egyptian deities typically had an associated cult, role and mythologies.
[
93

Pyramid texts
and ancient temples of Egypt, many

. Among these, were

(fertility god),

,

,

,

,

,

,

,

,

,

,

[

:

Most Egyptian deities represented natural phenomenon, physical objects or social aspects of life, as hidden immanent forces within these phenomena.
[

]
[

The deity

represented parts of the earth, and the god
Sia
represented the abstract powers of perception.
[

:

Deities such as

and

[

]

,

(singular

and the

revered both gods and goddesses.
